'''Anna Margaret Mullikin''' (1893–1975) was an American mathematician who was one of the early investigators of [[Connected space|point set theory]]. She was one of the few women to earn a PhD in math before World War II.<ref name="amm_2009">Bartlow, T. L. and [[David E. Zitarelli|Zitarelli, D. E.]] (2009) [http://www.maa.org/who-was-miss-mullikin-introduction ''Who Was Miss Mullikin?''], [[American Mathematical Monthly]] '''116'''(2), 99-114.</ref><ref name="nams_2009">Zitarelli, D. E. (2009) ''Connected Sets and the AMS: 1901-1921'', [[Notices of the American Mathematical Society]] '''56'''(4), 450-458.</ref><ref name=":0">[[Judy Green (mathematician)|Green, Judy]], Jeanne LaDuke: Pioneering Women in American Mathematics: The Pre-1940 PhD’s. 2009, {{ISBN|978-0-8218-4376-5}}</ref> 

== Biography ==
Anna Margaret Mullikin was born in [[Baltimore]], Maryland, March 7, 1893, as the youngest of four children of Sophia Ridgely (Battee) and William Lawrence Mullikin. Anna received her BA from [[Goucher College]], in [[Towson, Maryland|Towson]], Maryland, in 1915. After she graduated Mullikin taught in private schools including [[Science Hill School (Shelbyville, Kentucky)|Science Hill School]] in [[Shelbyville, Kentucky|Shelbyville]], Kentucky, (1915–1917) and at [[Mary Baldwin University|Mary Baldwin Seminary]] in [[Staunton, Virginia|Staunton]], Virginia, 1917–1918.<ref name=":0" /> 

Mullikin went on to attend [[University of Pennsylvania]] in [[Philadelphia]] for doctoral work. She was [[Robert Lee Moore]]'s third student, graduating with her PhD in 1922 with a dissertation titled ''Certain Theorems Relating to Plane Connected Point Sets''. Her dissertation was published that year in [[Transactions of the American Mathematical Society]]<ref name="tams_1922">Mullikin, A. (1922) ''Certain Theorems Relating to Plane Connected Point Sets'', [[Transactions of the American Mathematical Society]] '''24''', 144-162.</ref> and subsequently became the catalyst for significant advances in the field of topology.<ref name="amm_2009" /> Her main result was initially referred to as "Miss Mullikin's Theorem" but by 1928 it was called the "Janiszewski-Mullikin theorem."<ref name=":0" /> 

During 1921–1922, while studying for her doctorate, she taught at [[Oak Lane Day School|Oak Lane Country Day School]], which served preschool and elementary-aged children in Pennsylvania.<ref name=":1">{{citation|url=https://math.illinois.edu/system/files/inline-files/hamstrom_memoriam.pdf|title=In Memoriam: Mary-Elizabeth Hamstrom|publisher=University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign Department of Mathematics|first=John E.|last=Wetzel|magazine=Math Times|date=Spring 2010|pages=12–13}}. Also published as {{citation|url=https://www.news-gazette.com/obituaries/mary-elizabeth-hamstrom/article_20492ccc-c49f-5dba-8a4e-4589781650e4.html|title=Mary-Elizabeth Hamstrom|date=December 10, 2009|newspaper=News-Gazette}}.</ref>

As a PhD, she spent her career as a secondary school mathematics teacher, beginning at [[William Penn High School (Philadelphia)|William Penn High School]] in Philadelphia for one year (1922–1923) before moving to [[Germantown High School (Philadelphia)]]. There she became a mentor to [[Mary-Elizabeth Hamstrom]], who would go on to become a student of Moore and professional mathematician herself.<ref name=":1" /> At Germantown High School she was named department head of the mathematics in 1952, and she remained there until her retirement in 1959.<ref name=":0" />

Anna Mullikin died August 24, 1975, in Philadelphia at 82 and was interred in [[Mount Olivet Cemetery (Baltimore)|Mt. Olivet Cemetery]] in Baltimore, Maryland.<ref name=":0" />
